SUMMARY

Palo Alto(PANW+6.08%)reported fiscal first quarter results that exceeded management guidance across all key financial metrics, including revenue and Next-Generation Security ARR. The company announced a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock, a strategic move intended to expand its capabilities in post-training and inference for open weight AI models. Management reported record platformization activity and broad-based demand across its three primary segments: network and AI security, Cortex, and Idira. Following the quarter's performance, the company materially raised its full-year guidance for revenue and NGS ARR while maintaining its long-term profitability and free cash flow margin targets.

Hamza Fodderwala:Good day, everyone, and welcome to Palo Alto Networks' Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Conference Call. I'm Hamza Fodderwala, Senior Vice President and Head of Investor Relations. Please note that this call is being recorded today, Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 01:30 p.m. Pacific Time. With me on today's call to discuss our fiscal first quarter results are Nikesh Arora, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; and Dipak Golechha, our Chief Financial Officer. Following our prepared remarks, Lee Klarich, our Chief Product and Technology Officer, will join us for the question-and-answer portion. You can find the press release and other information to supplement today's discussion on our website at investors.paloaltonetworks.com.

While there, please click on the link for quarterly results to find the Q1 '27 supplemental financial information and Q1 '27 earnings presentation. During the course of today's call, we will be making forward-looking statements and projections regarding the company's business operations and financial performance as well as the company's recent acquisitions. These statements made today are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ from these forward-looking statements. Please review our press release and recent SEC filings for a description of these risks and uncertainties. We assume no obligation to update any forward-looking statements made in today's presentation.

This presentation also contains non-GAAP financial measures, and key metrics relating to the company's past and expected future performance. Non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered a substitute for financial measures prepared in accordance with GAAP. The most directly comparable GAAP financial measures and reconciliations are in the press release and the appendix of the investor presentation. Unless specifically noted otherwise, all results and comparisons are on a fiscal year-over-year basis. With that, I will now turn the call over to Nikesh.

Nikesh Arora:Thank you, Hamza. Good afternoon, everyone. As you can all see, we had a strong start to our first quarter of the fiscal year. We beat guidance across every metric. NGS ARR was up 66%, and we delivered 1 of the largest NGS ARR beats in our history. Total revenue was up 39%, and ARPU grew 35%, both of which accelerated versus the prior quarter. Delivering that kind of result in a seasonally slower Q1 speaks to the strength of the demand function. As AI accelerates cyber-attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms. That momentum gives us confidence to materially raise our guidance for the year.

Top line strength also translated directly to the bottom line. In Q1, we once again exceeded 30% operating margin, setting a new record for operating profitability while integrating large acquisitions. Most encouraging is how demand was broad-based across our platforms, all of which delivered accelerating revenue growth, starting with our largest business, network and AI security, which grew 20% with strength across SASE, software and hardware firewalls. Customers are moving beyond point products and recognizing that running fragmented perimeter defense across multiple vendors leaves critical gaps in visibility and enforcement. We're also seeing a fundamental shift in what traverses the network.

Agentic traffic on SASE is up approximately 9x year-over-year as autonomous agents continuously connect to applications, APIs and enterprise data, all of which require real-time inspection. That surge in traffic reflects enterprises moving AI into production, and securing this new surface area has propelled Prisma AIRS to nearly $170 million in ARR in 5 quarters since it was generally available, making it the fastest-growing product in the history of Palo Alto Networks. Cortex grew over 50% in Q1, led by XSIAM and observability. As AI-driven attacks move in machine speed, Band-Aid reactive solutions across multiple data lakes are not a plan.

We need solutions that run real-time analytics and observability, do dynamic correlation and are able to deliver real-time correlation and verdicts. XSIAM now in just over 20 petabytes of daily telemetry, leveraging AI to reduce response times from days to under 10 minutes. Turning to Idira, our identity security platform. Revenue here grew 23% in Q1 on a pro forma basis. We continue to execute on our integration plan since closing the CyberArk acquisition earlier this year. We added more than 100 net new logos from existing Palo Alto Networks installed base in Q1, our best cross-sell quarter to date between Idira and Palo Alto Networks.

The rise of AI agents introduces an entirely new class of nonhuman identities that must be secured in real time. Maintaining effective oversight requires complete visibility and the capability to instantly revoke access when suspicious activity occurs. To address this exact challenge, in Q1, we launched the general availability of Idira's agentic IdP, integrated directly into our Prisma AIRS AI gateway, enabling real-time enforcement against agentic permissions. Across all of the 3 platforms, customers are solving the same core problem, compressing the time between spotting, exposure and shutting it down. Point products simply cannot keep up when attacks move at machine speed.

Enterprises are responding by consolidating the security architecture onto unified platform, an ongoing shift that continues to provide momentum for platformization. Yes, that word platformization. In Q1, net new platformizations hit a record of approximately 170, which was more than the last 2 Q1s combined. Platformized customers now represent 2/3 of our next-generation security ARR and continue to expand at robust rate with net retention above 120%. Our largest deals detail the platformization strength we saw in the quarter. In Q1, we closed an $83 million deal with a global financial institution. This customer platformized on network security, adopting frontier virtual patching and expanded identity security, signing the largest ever deal in CyberArk history.

A global consulting firm signed a $46 million transaction, which included our largest ever Prisma AIRS deal, as they move AI into production across their organization. Finally, we signed a $20 million deal with a global IT services firm to help unify their security stack and reduce their point product sprawl and modernize their defenses. This customer purchased Prisma AIRS and SASE to secure AI deployments and access across their global workforce. Customers are making long-term architectural bets with us, and our responsibility grows with every commitment. They expect us to keep sharpening the products they rely on today while staying ahead of what comes next.

Six months ago, when cyber-capable models like Mythos were first released, we predicted that an equally powerful offensive AI capability would rapidly diffuse through open source within 3 to 6 months, prediction that has now materialized. And I want to be clear. There are 2 distinct parallel effects that are driving this environment. The first effect is a massive surge in vulnerabilities and patches being deployed. We're seeing critical and severe vulnerabilities discovered nearly 7x the monthly average of last year. These discoveries are happening at a speed and density, which is hard for IT teams to cope with.

We believe many of the major disruptions over the last few weeks including outages across major enterprises and governments were partially due to unintended consequence of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments. The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyber-attacks. Bad actors are using open weight models and new agentic frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale. New agentic frameworks like ARTEX are enabling bad actors to turn simple instructions into autonomous multistage attacks, allowing a handful of operators to compromise dozens of targets simultaneously.

We saw an example of that just days ago when our Unit 42 team published research on a campaign that involved a small team of foreign-linked hackers that were able to infiltrate 19 organizations at the same time. As we look ahead, we anticipate an elevated threat environment, but we believe enterprises have multiple ways to adapt to this new paradigm. First, the significant volume of patches will continue to be required for at least the next 18 months, carrying ongoing risks of collateral damage. We expect the collateral damage will decrease over time as customers get smarter about understanding exactly what to patch and when to patch.

Second, the need for virtual patching will grow across all industries and software categories, allowing organizations to securely and comfortably shield their infrastructure in line before applying their patch. In Q1, we saw strong demand for our advanced virtual patching service, and we see a large opportunity to deliver this to our nearly 70,000 network security customers. Third, the reality for every enterprise is that there's no silver bullet for preventing an attack, and organizations can no longer assume it won't happen to them. When an attack hits, because it will, defenders have to be ready to detect and remediate in record time rather than relying on reactive Band-Aids.

Therefore, we believe the third part of the antidote is most important, which is modernizing the north of $1 trillion of legacy security and IT infrastructure onto real-time platforms. Despite the heightened threat environment, demand for AI remains insatiable. Every drop in inference cost unlocks thousands of new agentic workflows, putting industry token revenue on a trajectory to surpass $1 trillion by 2029. While the market is focused on the AI trade, we are focused on the AI inflection, the shift from building AI infrastructure to real enterprise consumption. Until recently, most AI activity has been concentrated in consumer use cases and horizontal applications like coding, where there is virtually no security around these tokens.

Going forward, we believe the currently deployed AI infrastructure will also begin to show vulnerabilities, and we've seen recent examples of these exploits among AI infrastructure providers. As coding becomes more agentic, these lack of security controls will bring agentic risks into enterprise environments. It is imperative that we ensure AI adoption is in lockstep with AI security. We're already helping our customers close the gap with Prisma AIRS, reaching near $170 million in ARR across north of 1,000 customers within the last 5 quarters. Today, Prisma AIRS delivers comprehensive AI security across 5 pillars, giving enterprises a single platform to see, assess and control their entire AI footprint. It starts with AI discovery and AI risk assessment.

First, can you find every AI artifact in the enterprise? Prisma AIRS then discovers models and autonomous agents running anywhere, then continuously evaluates the risk across the supply chain, security posture and automated AI red teaming. From there, we move to real-time enforcement to AI protection and AI governance. Can you consolidate all that traffic into a single enforcement point? With on-time security, identity security and our AI gateway working together, customers inspect prompts, block sensitive data lakes, secure agent identities and enforce policy across every interaction in real time. This is the industry's first AI security platform.

And tying it all together is AI observability, capturing and observing every prompt, response and log so organizations maintain complete accountability at AI scale. While Prisma AIRS encompasses important pillars of AI security today, we expect that as models continue to get smarter, they will obviate static human controls. Because of this, AI security models will need to be equipped with advanced reasoning capabilities that are on par with the frontier. Trusting LLMs will require that we can independently verify, explain and audit AI implementations. We believe both trust and control will be essential to driving enterprise adoption of AI. We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open weight and open source models.

And early signs of that shift are clear, with open weight models growing from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year. When organizations put AI at the center of their operations, they want to retain control of their proprietary data, institutional judgment and competitive edge inside their own four walls. We expect a future with a serving opportunity in the hundreds of billions of dollars where enterprise applications are driven by open weight and open source adoption. Trust coupled with ability to control the AI implementation where it's both trainable and available on-prem or an assortment stack will accelerate enterprise adoption of AI.

That means that these models must be delivered securely and where required, in a sovereign fashion with controls strictly in the hands of the enterprise. When we looked at training custom open weight models ourselves, we looked at -- for partners across the entire AI ecosystem, looking for rare engineering rigor and a proven ability to address enterprise challenges. We landed on Applied Compute because no other team matched their technical pedigree in post-training open weight models. We are now bringing a world-class team of frontier AI researchers in-house and expect to reach 100 researchers by year-end. Every enterprise sits on decades of proprietary data, internal playbooks and institutional judgment that cannot be exposed to public models.

Until now, they have lacked a trusted partner to post-train run and supervise open weight models safely on their own. We believe Applied Compute is the right partner for us to address this opportunity. Team has already seen great traction with large enterprises and AI natives alike, achieving north of $100 million in annualized revenue with the last 18 months of founding, putting them in rarefied air. Applied Compute will allow us to execute on 2 major fronts. First, we will embed AI across all of our security capabilities and are in the process of training north of 35 specialized use cases and making them available to our customers to fight AI with AI.

Secondly, we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open weight models to the enterprise. Open weight model implementation will allow us to deliver secure open weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure enterprise -- secure AI in the enterprise. To support our efforts, we plan to build out a diversified global inference capability of north of 100-plus megawatts over the next 3 to 5 years. This will be supported by a modest CapEx commitment of least -- of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030, representing approximately half a year of our annual free cash flow.

By pairing their platform with our global go-to-market reach and the trust we have earned with CIOs worldwide, we expect Applied Compute to continue scaling rapidly and add over north of $1 billion of ARR to our next-generation security ARR by fiscal 2029. In closing, Q1 was a defining inflection point for cybersecurity. AI-driven attacks has stripped away the luxury of incremental change proving that fragmented decade-old tools cannot stop autonomous threats and creating an urgent mandate to modernize $1 trillion of legacy infrastructure. At the same time, to unleash AI adoption across the enterprise, AI security must evolve from visibility and enforcement to ensuring trust in the model itself.

Organizations will be reluctant to put mission-critical workflows on AI until they can rely on how those models behave in production. Lastly, we see a massive opportunity in enabling secure adoption of open weight models as sovereignty and control becoming pleasingly important pillars in the enterprise. By bringing that foundation to our customers alongside our core security platforms, we sit at the center of both their security modernization and their AI transformation for years to come. With that, I'll turn it over to Dipak to cover financial details in more depth and share our updated outlook.

Dipak Golechha:Thank you, Nikesh, and good afternoon, everyone. We delivered a record Q1 result with accelerating growth on all of our key top line metrics. RPO grew 35% year-over-year to $21.0 billion, Current RPO was up 36% year-over-year to $9.4 billion. Contract durations remained flat year-over-year. NGS ARR reached $9.73 billion, up 66% year-over-year, and net new NGS ARR more than doubled year-over-year. We significantly exceeded our guidance to deliver one of the highest quarterly NGS ARR beats in our history. Total revenue was up 39% year-over-year, reaching $3.44 billion in Q1. As we announced last quarter, we're now reporting revenue across our 3 segments: network and AI security, Cortex and Idira.

Q1 revenue performance was truly broad-based with all 3 of our segments delivering growth acceleration. On network and AI security, that delivered growth acceleration at scale in Q1 coming off a very strong Q4. Revenue grew 20% year-over-year to $2.3 billion. We saw strong growth across all form factors in network security. Starting with SASE, ARR grew 30% year-over-year, and we added over $100 million in net new NGS ARR. Demand was particularly strong for SD-WAN and secure browser as customers continue to favor our comprehensive SASE platform over point product vendors. In firewall, we saw strength across hardware and software with trailing 12-month bookings up 28% year-over-year.

We are continuing to gain share as the desire for unified visibility and prevention is driving vendor consolidation within our customer base. Software firewall ARR accelerated for the third consecutive quarter and grew 34% year-over-year. This was largely driven by Prisma AIRS, which continues to be our fastest-growing product, reaching nearly $170 million in ARR. Turning to Cortex, our security operations and observability platform. Q1 revenue grew 53% year-over-year and 40% year-over-year on a pro forma basis. XSIAM ARR grew over 65% year-over-year to approximately $800 million as customers prioritize their SOC modernization projects to combat the heightened threat environment driven by AI. Furthermore, our Observability platform, recently we launched as Cortex XCOR, continued its strong growth.

ARR was up approximately 4x year-over-year, and as we commented last quarter, that includes an approximately 9 figures of net new ARR from the large frontier lab customer migrating to Chronosphere from an incumbent provider. In Idira, our identity security platform, Q1 revenue grew 23% year-over-year on a pro forma basis. We continue to see strong go-to-market collaboration between our core sales team and Idira. In Q1, this resulted in over 100 net new logo wins for Idira, which came from our existing core installed base, representing our largest number of cross-sell wins since the acquisition closed. We're also seeing synergies -- strong synergies on the bottom line.

As a reminder, when we announced the acquisition, we targeted Idira operating margin converging with our core business within 18 to 24 months post close and are on track to do that in approximately half the time. From a geographic perspective, we saw broad-based strength. Americas grew 42% year-over-year. EMEA grew 40% year-over-year, and JAPAC grew 26% year-over-year. Complementing our record top line performance in Q1 was our continued focus on profitable growth. This discipline yielded continued operating leverage year-over-year, reinforcing our confidence in our margin guidance targets for the full year. Our scale, our diversified business model helps us mitigate gross margin headwinds, and we continue to deliver gross margin in the mid-70% range.

In Q1, our total gross margin was 75.2%, down 170 basis points year-over-year. As we noted last quarter, we continued to actively manage multiple factors impacting our gross margin over the near to medium term. First, we are seeing industry-wide elevated component costs within our hardware business, which we're proactively leveraging our scale and strategic supplier relationships. While hardware represents approximately 10% of our total revenue, we expect the elevated component costs to impact our gross margins throughout the course of the fiscal year. Second, our gross margins were impacted by a greater mix of higher growth SaaS offerings that are earlier in their maturity curve.

This is particularly true for the Cortex segment, where we are seeing our XSIAM and observability business grow rapidly as we focus on taking share. Additionally, our ongoing Prisma to Cortex Cloud migration remains a temporary drag on our segment margins. Given the migration and shifting product mix, we expect our gross margin in Cortex to remain below our overall company average over the medium term before returning to 70% plus gross margins longer term. From an operating margin standpoint, we continue to offset higher COGS with improving OpEx leverage as we scale efficiency. In Q1, our non-GAAP operating margin was 30.7%, a 50 basis point increase year-over-year despite higher costs related to M&A and gross margin impacts.

We are also driving a number of AI efficiency plays targeted in areas across our business. As an example, this includes our AI quoting efforts to accelerate our time to close in an effort to drive higher sales productivity. In addition, we're driving AI efficiencies in procurement and have already identified significant savings through our vendor rationalization efforts. Turning to the bottom line. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $1.05, up 13% year-over-year, beating guidance by $0.08; whilst EPS -- GAAP EPS was $0.57, up 21% year-over-year. Our improving profitability contributed to strong Q1 cash generation with adjusted free cash flow of $1.9 billion, representing a 56% margin.

Regarding capital allocation, we had no share repurchases in the quarter, and our approach continues to be opportunistic. We continue to have authorization of up to $1 billion in share repurchase until December 2027. Our overall performance is the direct result of our continued focus on innovation. Through organic investments and targeted M&A, we strive to continually stay ahead of technology inflections and anticipate our customers' needs years in advance. As Nikesh noted earlier, we're excited to announce our intent to acquire Applied Compute to position ourselves as the pioneer in delivering secure AI. The total consideration is $4.5 billion paid entirely in stock, and we expect to close in our third quarter of fiscal '27.

The acquisition includes approximately $500 million in cash and prepaid compute commitments owned by Applied Compute. The company has already achieved impressive growth, reaching $100 million in annualized revenue within 18 months of their founding. This transaction will be top line growth accretive from day 1, and we expect to scale the business to add $1 billion in NGS ARR by fiscal year '29. Longer term, we believe this is our next multibillion-dollar ARR business and positions us to be at the frontier of AI security.

While we expect our compute needs will grow to deliver secure post-training and inference for our customers, we intend to remain capital light, and we'll maintain strong free cash flow margins through and beyond the CapEx cycle. To meet our compute needs, we will continue to source from our cloud partners and over time, add dedicated capacity of our own. That investment will mostly go to GPUs and servers with a smaller share in the facilities that house them. We intend to build our capacity in stages against demand that we have visibility into.

In total, we anticipate our cumulative CapEx needs through fiscal 2030 to be less than $3 billion, which is approximately half of our expected free cash flow this year. Assuming a Q3 '27 close, we expect the transaction to lower our operating margin by up to 100 basis points in fiscal '27 and up to 200 basis points in fiscal '28 before returning to our current 29% to 30% operating margin in '29. Lastly, from a free cash flow perspective, we expect to maintain 38% plus margins excluding data center CapEx in fiscal '28 and beyond. We will provide more details and precise modeling points once we close the transactions. With that, I will turn to guidance.

Our guidance is for stand-alone Palo Alto Networks, excluding the pending Applied Compute acquisition. For the fiscal second quarter 2027, we expect NGS ARR between $10.2 billion to $10.22 billion or 61% growth, RPO between $21.5 billion to $21.6 billion or 35% to -- 34% to 35% growth, revenue between $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion or 36% to 37% growth, our fully diluted share count between 837 million to 842 million shares and our diluted non-GAAP EPS in the range of $1.01 to $1.03.

For the fiscal year 2027, we expect NGS ARR between $11.475 billion to $11.52 billion or 26% to 27% growth, RPO between $25.3 billion to $25.5 billion or 19% to 20% growth, revenue between $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion or 26% to 27% growth, our operating margin of 29.5%, diluted non-GAAP EPS in the range of $4.26 to $4.30 and our fully diluted share count between 844 million to 847 million shares. We expect our adjusted free cash flow margin of 38%. With that, I will turn it back over to Hamza for Q&A.

Hamza Fodderwala:All right. Thank you, Dipak. For our first question, we'll go to Saket Kalia from Barclays, followed by Brian Essex from JPMorgan.

Saket Kalia:Okay. Great. And congrats on a super strong start to the year. Really great to see. Nikesh, maybe for you. You've talked about the $1 trillion of tech debt for some time now. And maybe that feels even more relevant just given the outages that we've seen. Based on some of your recent customer conversations, where are CEOs and CIOs going to focus that modernization on most in 2027 as the new threat environment gets clearly more active?

Nikesh Arora:Saket, thanks for your question. Look, first and foremost, we're seeing a lot of interest in frontier AI defense. Almost every company is making sure that they're testing their infrastructure with pen testing, red teaming to make sure that all these new AI capabilities, they can inflict upon themselves before bad actors inflicted on them. I think the challenge, as we highlighted, right now is that there are so many vulnerabilities being discovered on a daily basis that it's impossible for enterprises to patch them. So I think they're -- bit of them are caught in the current sort of crisis at the moment, the short term.

There are people who are beginning to think about how does that impact their long-term architecture, and you can see that. That's reflected in the way we talked about platformizations. We've done 170 this quarter, which means people say, "Listen, I cannot manage a fragmented infrastructure. How do we get all this stuff put together?" The problem is whatever they do today is going to take 3 to 6 months, maybe 9 months, depending on how complex and how tired that environment is. So we're -- they're all embarking on that journey, and I think we're going to see more of that over the next foreseeable future.

Saket Kalia:Congrats again.

Hamza Fodderwala:All right. Thank you, Saket. Next, we'll go to Brian Essex from JPMorgan, followed by Rob Owens from Piper Sandler.

Brian Essex:Nikesh, for you, Would love to -- really interesting to see the acquisition. Would love to understand conversations with customers you've had that led to your interest in sovereign AI and maybe the nature of those conversations and how you're approaching AI sovereignty.

Nikesh Arora:That's a good question, Brian. Look, we started this journey where we said we have built Prisma AIRS. What Prisma AIRS does is it gives you visibility, shows you all the AI artifacts that you have in enterprise. That's easy to do. That's kind of deterministic. You can find it is discrete. Then we started to say can we bring all the traffic, so we can build an enforcement point and stop all this activity, bad activity from happening. And we figured out the common techniques of LLM sort of hacking through prompt injection, et cetera, and we built controls against that. That was also okay.

When the Hugging Face incident happened, it made us realize that we need to build something other than deterministic controls to intercept AI because deterministic controls cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct, every deception that it's going to try and do. We figured that it was not just to monitor to, say, fight AI with AI. We actually would have to have an LLM trained to interpret, understand and stop AI from misbehaving. And as we went on that journey, we started looking at, well, how do we go ahead and train models for ourselves.

And we went on a journey to look for multiple companies to see who could do it, and we looked at the capabilities across the market, and Applied Compute stood out. And then we came with a conclusion that as we train our models for enterprise applications, you will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time. So it's almost like having AI -- build AI and have -- build AI that watches this AI. You can't do it independently. I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else's application because I don't know how it's supposed to behave because I didn't train it.

So imagine if you can train your application and have the same team train something that supervises the application. I think that's the future of AI security. So in that context, we have to get in the training business to be able to build a good supervision business. And that's our bet. And we were delighted the Applied Compute team thought that was the right idea. We're excited at what got the deal sort of done and announced today. And I think it's going to be a huge opportunity.

In fact, while I'm sitting here, I had a CEO text me saying he met them this morning, and he's really excited now that their concern would have been how do we go to a small team of 100 people and entrust our large enterprise application on them. Now they feel, with Palo Alto behind them, they can rest assured that this is going to be a long-term play for them. So I'm very excited. Hopefully, this is the right bet for us. And if it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do today.

Hamza Fodderwala:Next, we'll go to Rob Owens from Piper Sandler, followed by Meta Marshall from Morgan Stanley. Rob you're on? Okay. Maybe we'll go to the next person in the queue. We'll go to Meta Marshall from Morgan Stanley, followed by Patrick Colville from Scotiabank.

Meta Marshall:Maybe I just wanted to ask, Nikesh, how you think customers are handling the fact that some of those virtual patching or accelerated hatching is clearly causing more outages just as there are errors kind of as they bring some of this online. So do you see kind of a slowdown? Do you see some form of grouping? Do you see more kind of services involvement? Just how do you see kind of the pickup in outages changing how the patching process is going to go?

Nikesh Arora:Going to call a friend.

Lee Klarich:Thank you, Nikesh. Thank you for the question. Let me first separate the 2 things that you just mentioned. The virtual patching is actually the solution to the challenges associated with patching too quickly and some of the operational impact that comes with that. So take a step back. All of the vulnerabilities that are being found by AI is creating this new wave of patches. That wave of patches then drives the operational challenge of how fast can companies patch everything that they have.

And that is what is putting the strain on operations teams, and that is what then leads to some of the types of outages we've been seeing recently, is just organizations trying to move too fast on applying the patches. What virtual patching allows is for companies to have a mitigation that is safe to deploy, giving their operations teams time to actually apply the real patches. And so what, in essence, we're able to provide is the security they need real time and immediate to the vulnerabilities being discovered, giving them time for the patches to be applied.

And to put this in context, our virtual packaging already has thousands of virtual patches as part of the service by the end of this calendar year. We expect that to be tens of thousands, and it's ramping up very quickly to keep pace with the vulnerabilities that are being discovered.

Hamza Fodderwala:Thank you, Meta. Next, we'll go to Patrick Colville from Scotiabank, followed by Shaul Eyal from Cowen.

Patrick Colville:I guess, Nikesh and possibly Dipak as well, I wanted to stick on this theme of the real-world impacts from the heightened cyber risk. In our latest conversations with your largest customers, it's clear that continuous frontier AI defense is like white-hot as a product. And so I guess, just want to hear a little bit of where you think the scope of this product could be. Is it something that is applicable to all enterprises, mid and large? Is this going to be a category that could mature into like a pretty substantial category? Or is it a November 2026 kind of pain point seeing spend but might level out over time?

Nikesh Arora:It has been a notion of vulnerability management historically, which was an industry TAM, which was more sort of a set of professionals finding vulnerabilities, institutionalizing them and selling them as feeds for others to be able to go look at their infrastructure and match them. Now what's happened is with the capabilities we've seen with frontier LLMs in the last few months, is that it's become an institutionalized capability, which you don't need to go send -- outsource and you can custom check your infrastructure and configuration that, unfortunately, is in such a way that bad actors can do it.

So there's a mad rush for every enterprise to go make sure that they have a robust perimeter, robust infrastructure to make sure they don't get breached. There's a mad rush of vendors to make sure that they can plug any holes from a vulnerability perspective. I think the progression in the last 6 months has been such that a lot more are getting found now with the most recent models than there were 6 months ago, so I don't think the capabilities of the model has plateaued yet.

And I don't expect it will plateau for another 6 to 9 months, which means you will keep getting better models over the next 6 to 9 months, smarter models, which you'll find much more sort of can do much more from a simulation perspective, find your attack paths. So I think for the next 12 months, or pick your number, 12 to 18 months, there is going to be the need for persistent fronter AI testing, which is why we call it continuous frontier AI defense because we don't think it's going to stop in the short term.

I do believe from an industry structure perspective, over time, the continuous frontier defense will morph into a capability that every company would have delivered to them by their platform providers, whether it's through our XSIAM platform, through our perimeter security platform because our platforms will have to constantly check and stress test their infrastructure and start self-healing over time as opposed to expecting them to find them and then get -- talk to us about fixing it. So you feel all of us in the industry will absorb that into our capabilities.

Nikesh Arora:Good strategy.
